subject: english-language
title: Numbers and Threes
welcome_lead: Statistics and triplets — the last two letters of AFOREST.
meta_desc: KS3 English Language adventure on statistics and triplets in persuasion.
final_note: You can now use stats and rule of three to strengthen writing.

walkthroughs.body_html: '92% of teachers agree' uses a statistic to lend authority. Use sparingly — too many numbers blur.
Triplets echo speeches and adverts: 'stop, look, listen' — 'tired, hungry, hopeful'. Three items lodge in memory.
Direct address uses 'you' to involve the reader: 'You can change this today.' Persuades by personal call.

mcqs.q: Groups of three for impact are called.
What is the difference between a dialect and an accent?
options: A dialect is a foreign language; an accent is how locals speak.
A noun phrase is a sentence that contains nouns.
Dialect and accent mean the same thing.
Accent refers only to pronunciation; dialect includes vocabulary and grammar as well as pronunciation — so all dialects involve accents but not vice versa.

mcqs.q: Why does English vocabulary have so many synonyms?
options: English has many synonyms because Shakespeare invented lots of words.
Because English speakers have always wanted to make things complicated.
Layered historical contact — Old English, Old Norse, Norman French and Latin — left English with multiple words from different sources for similar concepts (e.g. ask/question/interrogate).
A dialect is a foreign language; an accent is how locals speak.
A noun phrase is just a noun by itself.
A dialect is a foreign language; an accent is how locals speak.
A syntactic unit headed by a noun, which may include determiners, adjectives and modifiers — e.g. 'the big red car' is a noun phrase functioning as a single grammatical unit.
A noun phrase is a sentence that contains nouns.
